q: We recognise gases, liquids and solids quite easily because an important example of each is all around us: air, water and ____.
e: We recognise gases, liquids and solids quite easily because an important example of each is all around us: air, water and soil. Air, water and soil are the everyday gas, liquid and solid sitting around us.

q: The ____ state is the simplest state of matter to understand.
e: The gaseous state is the simplest state of matter to understand. The gaseous state is the simplest to understand because particles are far apart and attractions are weak. Among the three states, the gas model is the easiest because particles are far apart with weak forces.

q: ____ gas is required to keep our bodies alive.
e: Oxygen gas is required to keep our bodies alive. Cells use oxygen in respiration to stay alive, so that is the gas the body cannot do without. nitrogen is plentiful in air but does not keep cells alive.

q: Carbon dioxide is a gas given off as waste by animals and used as a raw material by ____.
e: Carbon dioxide is a gas given off as waste by animals and used as a raw material by plants. Animals give off carbon dioxide, and plants take that gas as a raw material for photosynthesis.

q: ____ gas is used as fuel.
e: Methane gas is used as fuel. Methane is the hydrocarbon gas burned as a fuel.

q: Ammonia gas which is a combination of nitrogen and hydrogen gases is used to make ____.
e: Ammonia gas which is a combination of nitrogen and hydrogen gases is used to make fertiliser. Ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen and is the feedstock for nitrogen fertiliser. Ammonia is NH3, a combination of nitrogen with hydrogen.

q: Thus, it is important to study the behaviour of gases and their ____.
e: Thus, it is important to study the behaviour of gases and their reactions. Gas behaviour and gas reactions both matter because so much chemistry happens in the gas phase.

q: The volume and shape of all gases can be assumed as those of their ____.
e: The volume and shape of all gases can be assumed as those of their containers. A gas has no shape or volume of its own, so it takes the shape and volume of its container.

q: The intermolecular forces of gases are much ____ than those of other physical states.
e: The intermolecular forces of gases are much weaker than those of other physical states. Intermolecular forces in a gas are weak because the particles sit far apart compared with a liquid or solid.

q: Being the most ____ of the states of matter, they can be mixed evenly and completely when confined to the same container.
e: Being the most compressible of the states of matter, they can be mixed evenly and completely when confined to the same container. Gases are the most compressible state because most of the volume is empty space between particles.

q: Gases have much ____ densities than liquids and solids.
e: Gases have much lower densities than liquids and solids. Gas density is low because a small mass is spread through a large empty volume.

q: The ____ is a model that is used to predict gas behaviour.
e: The Kinetic Molecular Theory is a model that is used to predict gas behaviour. The kinetic molecular theory treats a gas as tiny particles in constant random motion with lots of empty space between them.

q: The volume of the particles themselves is ____ compared with the total volume of the gas.
e: The volume of the particles themselves is negligible compared with the total volume of the gas. The particles' own volume is negligible next to the volume of the gas, which is mostly empty space.

q: Most of the volume of the gas is ____ space.
e: Most of the volume of the gas is empty space. Most of a gas's volume is empty space, so the particles themselves take up a negligible share.

q: Gas molecules are in constant motion in ____ directions, and they frequently collide with one another.
e: Gas molecules are in constant motion in random directions, and they frequently collide with one another. Gas particles travel in random straight-line bursts and change direction only when they collide.

q: Collisions among molecules are perfectly ____.
e: Collisions among molecules are perfectly elastic. Elastic collisions keep the total kinetic energy of the particles. energy is not lost as heat in the ideal-gas picture.

q: In other words, energy can be ____ from one molecule to another as a result of a collision.
e: In other words, energy can be transferred from one molecule to another as a result of a collision. One mole is the amount that holds as many particles as 12 g of carbon-12, which is 6.02 x 10^23 particles. Energy can move from one molecule to another in a collision, while the total for the system stays the same.

q: the total energy of all the molecules in a system remains the ____.
e: The total energy of all the molecules in a system remains the same. Ideal-gas collisions are elastic, so the total kinetic energy of the molecules stays the same.

q: Gas molecules exert neither attractive nor ____ forces on one another.
e: Gas molecules exert neither attractive nor repulsive forces on one another. Ideal gas particles are treated as having no attractions or repulsions, only collisions.

q: The average kinetic energy of molecules is the same for all gases at the same ____.
e: The average kinetic energy of molecules is the same for all gases at the same temperature. Kelvin temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the gas particles.

q: its value is directly proportional to the ____ temperature.
e: Its value is directly proportional to the Kelvin temperature. Gas laws use Kelvin because that scale starts at absolute zero, where particle motion would stop.

q: For any trapped sample of gas, we can measure its temperature, the volume of the space it occupies, its pressure against the confining wall and its ____.
e: For any trapped sample of gas, we can measure its temperature, the volume of the space it occupies, its pressure against the confining wall and its mass. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws.

q: The units of temperature are degree Celsius, degree Fahrenheit and ____.
e: The units of temperature are degree Celsius, degree Fahrenheit and Kelvin. Gas laws use Kelvin because that scale starts at absolute zero, where particle motion would stop.

q: The boiling point of water is ____ $^{\circ} C$.
e: The boiling point of water is 100 ^ degrees C. The boiling point of water is ^ degrees C.

q: normal human body temperature is ____ $^{\circ} C$.
e: Normal human body temperature is 37 ^ degrees C. Normal human body temperature is ^ degrees C.

q: Absolute zero is ____ K.
e: Absolute zero is 0 K. Absolute zero is 0 K, the point where gas volume in Charles's law would theoretically hit zero. That temperature is also -273 degrees C on the Celsius scale.
1000 cm^3 = 1000 mL = 1 L = 1 dm^3. One litre is the same volume as one cubic decimetre, which is also 1000 mL or 1000 cm3.

q: A gas exerts a ____ on the walls of any container.
e: A gas exerts a force on the walls of any container. A gas has no shape or volume of its own, so it takes the shape and volume of its container.

q: Pressure is in fact the force that acts on a given ____.
e: Pressure is in fact the force that acts on a given area. Gas pressure is the force of collisions on a unit area of the wall.

q: 1 $Nm^{-2}$ = 1 Pa (____ is SI unit of pressure).
e: 1 Nm^-2 = 1 Pa (pascal is SI unit of pressure). The SI unit of pressure is the pascal, one newton per square metre.

q: The effects of pressure are observed in the mixture of gases surrounding the Earth-our ____.
e: The effects of pressure are observed in the mixture of gases surrounding the Earth-our atmosphere. The mixture of gases around Earth is the atmosphere, and that mixture exerts pressure.

q: The atmosphere is composed of nitrogen, oxygen, ____ and other minor constituents.
e: The atmosphere is composed of nitrogen, oxygen, argon and other minor constituents. About 78 percent of clean dry air is nitrogen.

q: The actual value of atmospheric pressure depends on location, temperature and ____ conditions.
e: The actual value of atmospheric pressure depends on location, temperature and weather conditions. Atmospheric pressure changes with location, temperature and weather.

q: Instruments used for measuring atmospheric pressure and gas pressure are barometer and ____, respectively.
e: Instruments used for measuring atmospheric pressure and gas pressure are barometer and manometer, respectively. A barometer measures atmospheric pressure, and a manometer measures the pressure of a confined gas. A manometer measures gas pressure by comparing it with atmospheric pressure.

q: Standard atmospheric pressure (1 atm) is equal to the pressure that supports a column of ____ exactly 760 mm high at 0 $^{\circ} C$ at sea level.
e: Standard atmospheric pressure (1 atm) is equal to the pressure that supports a column of mercury exactly 760 mm high at 0 ^ degrees C at sea level. One atmosphere is 101325 pascals, newtons per square metre.

q: The mmHg unit is also the same as the ____.
e: The mmHg unit is also the same as the torr. The torr is defined to be equal to one millimetre of mercury.

q: 1 atm = ____ Pa.
e: 1 atm = 101,325 Pa. One atmosphere is 101325 pascals, newtons per square metre. A pascal is one newton of force on each square metre.

q: The mass of a gas can be determined by weighing the gas in an enclosed container by gram or ____.
e: The mass of a gas can be determined by weighing the gas in an enclosed container by gram or kilogram. A gas has no shape or volume of its own, so it takes the shape and volume of its container. The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram, symbol kg.

q: In spite of wide differences in chemical properties, all the gases more or less obey the ____ laws.
e: In spite of wide differences in chemical properties, all the gases more or less obey the gas laws. The gas laws still describe pressure, volume and temperature even when the gases differ chemically.

q: The gas laws deal with how gases behave with respect to pressure, volume, temperature and ____.
e: The gas laws deal with how gases behave with respect to pressure, volume, temperature and amount. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws.

q: Boyle's law can be stated as: When the temperature of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the volume of the gas is ____ proportional to its pressure.
e: Boyle's law can be stated as: When the temperature of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the volume of the gas is inversely proportional to its pressure. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws. Boyle's law keeps temperature and amount fixed, so pressure and volume move in opposite directions.

q: In the 17th century, Robert Boyle, an Irish scientist, studied the behaviour of gases systematically and ____.
e: In the 17th century, Robert Boyle, an Irish scientist, studied the behaviour of gases systematically and quantitatively. Boyle's law keeps temperature and amount fixed, so pressure and volume move in opposite directions. Gas behaviour and gas reactions both matter because so much chemistry happens in the gas phase.

q: where $P_1$ and $V_1$ are for the ____ conditions.
e: Where P_1 and V_1 are for the initial conditions. Where P_1 and V_1 are for the conditions.

q: Charles' law can be stated as: When the pressure of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the volume of the gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the ____ scale.
e: Charles' law can be stated as: When the pressure of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the volume of the gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the Kelvin scale. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws. Gay-Lussac's pressure-temperature law says pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature at constant volume. Charles's law keeps pressure and amount fixed, so volume rises in step with Kelvin temperature.

q: In the 18th century, the French physicist ____ studied the effect of temperature on the volume of a gas at constant pressure.
e: In the 18th century, the French physicist Jacques Charles studied the effect of temperature on the volume of a gas at constant pressure. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws. Charles's law keeps pressure and amount fixed, so volume rises in step with Kelvin temperature.

q: Absolute zero temperature: The volume of a given mass of gas decreases regularly with a regular decrease in ____.
e: Absolute zero temperature: The volume of a given mass of gas decreases regularly with a regular decrease in temperature. Absolute zero is 0 K, the point where gas volume in Charles's law would theoretically hit zero.

q: If the constant contraction rate is continued, the volume of the gas will become zero at ____ $^{\circ} C$.
e: If the constant contraction rate is continued, the volume of the gas will become zero at -273 ^ degrees C. The volume of the gas will become zero at -273 ^ degrees C.

q: This temperature is taken as the zero point of a new scale of temperature(Kelvin temperature scale), and is also known as ____ zero temperature.
e: This temperature is taken as the zero point of a new scale of temperature(Kelvin temperature scale), and is also known as absolute zero temperature. Gas laws use Kelvin because that scale starts at absolute zero, where particle motion would stop. Absolute zero is 0 K, the point where gas volume in Charles's law would theoretically hit zero.

q: Gay-Lussac's law can be stated as: When a ____ of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the pressure of the gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the Kelvin scale.
e: Gay-Lussac's law can be stated as: When a volume of a given mass of gas is kept constant, the pressure of the gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the Kelvin scale. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws. Gay-Lussac's pressure-temperature law says pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature at constant volume. Gay-Lussac's law keeps volume and amount fixed, so pressure rises in step with Kelvin temperature.

q: Early in the 19th century, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac, a French scientist, determined that the pressure of a gas sample increases when heated and decreases when ____ at constant volume.
e: Early in the 19th century, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac, a French scientist, determined that the pressure of a gas sample increases when heated and decreases when cooled at constant volume. Gay-Lussac's law keeps volume and amount fixed, so pressure rises in step with Kelvin temperature.

q: STP in chemistry is the abbreviation for Standard Temperature and ____.
e: STP in chemistry is the abbreviation for Standard Temperature and Pressure. At STP you compare gases at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atm, where one mole occupies 22.4 L. Standard temperature and pressure let you compare gas amounts using a shared 22.4 L molar volume.

q: STP is commonly used when calculating gas density and ____ of gas.
e: STP is commonly used when calculating gas density and volume of gas. Gas density is low because a small mass is spread through a large volume of empty space. At STP you compare gases at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atm, where one mole occupies 22.4 L.

q: standard temperature = 0 $^{\circ} C$(or) ____ K.
e: Standard temperature = 0 ^ degrees C(or) 273 K. Standard temperature and pressure let you compare gas amounts using a shared 22.4 L molar volume.

q: room temperature = ____ $^{\circ} C$(or) 298 K.
e: Room temperature = 25 ^ degrees C(or) 298 K. Room temperature = ^ degrees Cor 298 K.

q: There is a single expression, called the Combined Gas Law that combines Boyle's Law, Charles' Law and ____ Law.
e: There is a single expression, called the Combined Gas Law that combines Boyle's Law, Charles' Law and Gay-Lussac's Law. Boyle's law keeps temperature and amount fixed, so pressure and volume move in opposite directions. Charles's law keeps pressure and amount fixed, so volume rises in step with Kelvin temperature.

q: When only the ____ of gas is constant, the combined gas law describes the relationship among pressure(P), volume (V) and temperature (T).
e: When only the amount of gas is constant, the combined gas law describes the relationship among pressure(P), volume (V) and temperature (T). Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws.

q: Gay-Lussac studied the volume relationship of reacting gases, and summarised the results known as Gay-Lussac's law of combining ____ of gases.
e: Gay-Lussac studied the volume relationship of reacting gases, and summarised the results known as Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes of gases. Gay-Lussac's law keeps volume and amount fixed, so pressure rises in step with Kelvin temperature. Gay-Lussac's combining-volumes law says gas volumes in a reaction sit in simple whole-number ratios at the same T and P.

q: At the same temperature and pressure, the volumes of reacting gases and gaseous products are in simple ratios of small ____ numbers.
e: At the same temperature and pressure, the volumes of reacting gases and gaseous products are in simple ratios of small whole numbers. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws.

q: The Italian scientist ____ expressed that the volume of any given gas must be proportional to the number of moles or molecules present.
e: The Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro expressed that the volume of any given gas must be proportional to the number of moles or molecules present. Avogadro's law says equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules. Avogadro's number is about 6.02 x 10^23 particles in one mole. Avogadro links gas volume at the same T and P to the number of particles, and one mole holds 6.02 x 10^23 of them.

q: At constant temperature and pressure, the volume, V, occupied by a gas sample is directly proportional to the number of ____, n, of gas.
e: At constant temperature and pressure, the volume, V, occupied by a gas sample is directly proportional to the number of moles, n, of gas. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws. Gay-Lussac's pressure-temperature law says pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature at constant volume.

q: Under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, equal volumes of all gases contain the same number of ____.
e: Under the same conditions of temperature and pressure, equal volumes of all gases contain the same number of molecules. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws.

q: equal volumes of all gases contain the same number of molecules (or atoms if the gas is ____).
e: Equal volumes of all gases contain the same number of molecules (or atoms if the gas is monoatomic). Number of molecules or atoms if the gas.

q: The proportionality constant (R) is called the ____ constant.
e: The proportionality constant (R) is called the gas constant. (R) is called the gas constant.

q: This equation is known as the ____ law equation.
e: This equation is known as the ideal gas law equation. An ideal gas is the model where particle volume and attractions are ignored so pressure, volume and temperature follow a clean equation.

q: For 1 mol of gas at standard temperature and pressure, the volume is ____ L.
e: For 1 mol of gas at standard temperature and pressure, the volume is 22.4 L. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws. Standard temperature and pressure let you compare gas amounts using a shared 22.4 L molar volume.

q: The value of the gas constant 'R' depends on the units used for pressure, volume and ____.
e: The value of the gas constant 'R' depends on the units used for pressure, volume and temperature. Pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed amount of gas are tied together by the gas laws.

q: An ideal gas is a ____ gas.
e: An ideal gas is a hypothetical gas. An ideal gas is the model where particle volume and attractions are ignored so pressure, volume and temperature follow a clean equation.

q: The molecules of an ideal gas do not attract or ____ one another.
e: The molecules of an ideal gas do not attract or repel one another. An ideal gas is the model where particle volume and attractions are ignored so pressure, volume and temperature follow a clean equation.

q: the ideal gas molecules are approximated as ____ particles that have no volume in and of themselves.
e: The ideal gas molecules are approximated as point particles that have no volume in and of themselves. An ideal gas is the model where particle volume and attractions are ignored so pressure, volume and temperature follow a clean equation.

q: Although real gases differ mostly from ideal gas behaviour at low temperatures and ____ pressures
e: Although real gases differ mostly from ideal gas behaviour at low temperatures and high pressures. An ideal gas is the model where particle volume and attractions are ignored so pressure, volume and temperature follow a clean equation.

q: the particles in a real gas have volume, and there are ____ between the particles.
e: The particles in a real gas have volume, and there are attractions between the particles. Real gases deviate from the ideal model because the particles have volume and attractions.

q: a real gas can condense, or even ____, when it is compressed or cooled.
e: A real gas can condense, or even solidify, when it is compressed or cooled. Real gases deviate from the ideal model because the particles have volume and attractions.

q: the real gases behave mostly like an ideal gas at high temperatures and ____ pressures.
e: The real gases behave mostly like an ideal gas at high temperatures and low pressures. An ideal gas is the model where particle volume and attractions are ignored so pressure, volume and temperature follow a clean equation.

q: the ideal gas works rather well for most reasonable temperature and ____ ranges.
e: The ideal gas works rather well for most reasonable temperature and pressure ranges. An ideal gas is the model where particle volume and attractions are ignored so pressure, volume and temperature follow a clean equation.

q: In practice, chemists often deal with the ____ gases.
e: In practice, chemists often deal with the unknown gases. In practice, chemists often deal with the gases.

q: To determine the molar mass of an unknown gas, chemists need to determine the ____ of gas experimentally and use the rearranged ideal gas law.
e: To determine the molar mass of an unknown gas, chemists need to determine the density of gas experimentally and use the rearranged ideal gas law. Gas density is low because a small mass is spread through a large volume of empty space. An ideal gas is the model where particle volume and attractions are ignored so pressure, volume and temperature follow a clean equation. q: Dalton's law of partial pressures can be stated as: When the temperature is kept constant, the total pressure of a gas mixture is the ____ of the partial pressures of different gases.
e: Dalton's law of partial pressures can be stated as: When the temperature is kept constant, the total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of different gases. Dalton's law adds the partial pressures of gases in a mixture to get the total pressure. Partial pressure is the pressure one gas would exert if it occupied the container alone.

q: In the early 19th century, the English chemist, ____ formulated the law for the pressure of the mixture of non-reacting gases.
e: In the early 19th century, the English chemist, John Dalton formulated the law for the pressure of the mixture of non-reacting gases. Dalton's law adds the partial pressures of gases in a mixture to get the total pressure.

q: Each gas in the mixture exerts a pressure that is ____ of the other gases present.

e: Due to their molecular motions, gases have the property of diffusion. the ability of two or more gases to mix spontaneously until they form a uniform mixture.

e: Thus, diffusion is the gradual mixing of molecules of one gas with molecules of another by virtue of their kinetic properties. Diffusion is the spreading of gas particles from higher to lower concentration through random motion.

q: Effusion is the process by which a gas under pressure escapes from one ____ of a container to another by passing through a small opening.
e: Effusion is the process by which a gas under pressure escapes from one compartment of a container to another by passing through a small opening.
